idiom_name: WeakMap / WeakSet keyed by object identity (ES2015); WeakRef + FinalizationRegistry for weak values
implementation_notes: Weak references are built into the language: WeakMap holds object or non-registered-symbol keys weakly (a value becomes collectable once its key is), WeakSet does the same for elements, and since ES2021 WeakRef.deref() exposes a target that may already be gone, with FinalizationRegistry as the cleanup notification. WeakMap is the right tool for side data, per-object metadata and object-keyed registries because it cannot pin its keys and is deliberately not enumerable - no size(), no iteration - while WeakRef is for caches whose key is a string and whose value is large, paired with a strong Map and a registry entry to delete dead entries. MDN states the discipline plainly: WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry offer introspection into the collector, are best avoided, and must never carry program logic.
pitfalls: Collection timing is not guaranteed: a target may never be reclaimed while the program lives, and a target created or dereferenced in the current job cannot be reclaimed before that job ends - never make correctness depend on a WeakRef being cleared.
WeakMap holds keys weakly but values strongly, so a value that references its own key keeps the pair alive - the classic pinned-entry leak.

A WeakRef target cannot be changed, a deref result is not kept alive beyond the current job, and FinalizationRegistry callbacks are never synchronous: the object may already be gone when the callback runs.

WeakMap keys must be objects or non-registered symbols, and WeakMap/WeakSet expose no size() and no iteration, so primitives cannot be keys and stale entries cannot be discovered by walking the collection.

variants.name: WeakRef + FinalizationRegistry value cache
variants.idiom_name: Strong Map of WeakRef values swept by a FinalizationRegistry
variants.implementation_notes: The ES2021 pair covers what WeakMap cannot: a cache keyed by a string or another primitive whose values are large objects held weakly. Keep a normal Map from key to WeakRef, deref on every read and recompute on a miss, and register each value with a FinalizationRegistry whose callback deletes the entry - after re-checking that the WeakRef is still empty, or the callback may delete a newer live entry stored under the same key. Both APIs are explicitly non-deterministic, so they belong to memory optimisation in long-running programs, never to correctness.
pitfalls: The registry callback must re-check the WeakRef before deleting, or it can drop a live entry that was re-inserted under the same key after the old value died.
Nothing guarantees the callback runs at all (or before shutdown), so entries may stay stale - the cache needs a sweep or a size bound of its own.
deref() is a snapshot for the current job: the engine is free to reclaim the target immediately after the call returns, so hold the deref result in a local while using it.
